title: The stone under the rice
hook: a plate heaped with rice, and a stone hidden under it: the Kashmiri poet Lal Ded, and the one word her teacher gave her
carry: the guru's one word: turn within

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sharana takes refuge in God alone: Akka asked for her alms to fall and a dog to take them, and ended on the lord white as jasmine.
screen: `A SHARANA TAKES REFUGE IN GOD ALONE.`

segments.voice: Dinner is served, and the young wife's plate looks generous, a full mound of rice. Only she knows what's underneath: a stone, with the rice spread thin over it, so the plate looks full while there's hardly anything to eat. Kashmiris tell this story about a young bride named Lalla and the mother-in-law who, tradition says, served her this way. She doesn't complain. She eats what there is, washes the stone, and sets it back. In time she would leave that house and become the poet Kashmir remembers as Lal Ded.
screen: `A FULL PLATE OF RICE.` → `A STONE UNDERNEATH.` → `THE BRIDE WHO BECAME LAL DED.`

segments.voice: She goes by more than one name: Lalla, Lalleshwari, and Lal Ded, the one Kashmir knows best. She sang in Kashmiri, not Sanskrit, in short sayings called vakhs, easy to remember and pass from mouth to mouth. The stories say that after years of hardship at home she walked out as a wandering seeker, and found a teacher. Then comes a saying about that teacher, in paraphrase. My teacher gave me only one word. He said: from outside, go within. That one word became my rule, and so I began to dance, with nothing on. Notice how little she was given. Not a library, not a long course of rituals. One word. That's still how many Hindus receive a path: from a guru, at initiation, diksha, often as one short word or mantra, given in person and kept for life. And she didn't argue with it or add to it. She took it all the way. If what matters is within, then the outside, even the clothes, stops being the point. The stone story fits: a plate that looks full and isn't, and a bride who keeps quiet, because what feeds her isn't on the plate. Some readers hear her saying as a teaching about Shiva, found inside, the way some Shaiva teachers in Kashmir speak of him. This season, four days with her, starting with the one word.
screen: `A POET OF MANY NAMES` · `SHORT SAYINGS IN KASHMIRI` · `ONE WORD: GO WITHIN` · `WHAT'S UNDER THE RICE`

segments.voice: Notice where your attention points right now: at sounds, at the screen, at the next thing to do. Then gently turn it around, from outside in, and feel the breath at the tip of the nose, then in the chest; when the mind runs back outside, and it will, turn it in again. If you have a mantra from a teacher or your family, say it silently there. If you pray, look for God within, in your own way.
Lal Ded. The Kashmiri poet whose teacher gave her one word, from outside, go within, and who took it all the way. Today's word.
Your line: the guru's one word, turn within. One word was enough, taken all the way. See you tomorrow.

notes: The stone-under-the-rice story is a traditional legend, told here as such; confirm its usual shape (stone covered with rice, Lalla washing it and returning it).

Vakh paraphrase: confirm against Grierson and Barnett's Lalla-Vakyani (the guru's single precept, 'from without enter within', and her dancing naked). Not quoted because the exact 1920 wording could not be verified.
'Lal Ded, which tradition hears as Granny Lal': confirm the gloss of 'Ded' (grandmother/elder woman).
The link to Kashmir's Shaiva teachers is kept general; a Keeper may want to name Kashmir Shaivism more precisely or leave it out.
howItsDone says she is remembered by Kashmiris of more than one faith (Hindu Lalleshwari, Muslim Lalla Arifa); confirm wording.
Original: लल्लेश्वरी (Lalleshwari) in Devanagari; confirm spelling. Kashmiri has also been written in Sharada and Perso-Arabic scripts.
Editor pass: cut the 'Granny Lal' gloss of Ded (etymology), 'one of her best-known sayings' (superlative), and told the stone story as story; softened the Kashmir Shaiva attribution.
